safe_wording: A running refrigerator gets rid of heat through its outside. Depending on the design, the condenser is a coil on the back, tubing hidden inside the side walls, or a fan-cooled coil in a compartment at the bottom, and many models also run warm refrigerant tubing around the door openings. In a hot room the sides of some models can get hotter than 50 °C (about 120 °F).

allowed_numbers.how_to_say_it: in a hot room the sides of some fridges can get hotter than 50 °C (about 120 °F)

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: 'heat dissipation pipes are installed along the outer walls'
Hot-wall serpentine welded to side-wall lining plate; external condenser in direct contact with ambient; hot-wall 'commonly found in refrigerators produced in North America'
Fan mounted in the machine compartment with the condenser
'The condenser is located under the cabinet bottom.'; perimeter hot tube
'Condenser is installed on the back or both sides of refrigerator'; sides about 50-55 degC when ambient above 35 degC
Coils located at the bottom in most newer models, otherwise on the rear
Normal operation: 'The two sides can reach a temperature of 131 °F, or 55 °C.'
Hot refrigerant gas tubing around the cabinet door opening

problems: Haier's surface temperatures contradict each other across Haier's own regional pages. India: about 40 degC normal, 60-65 degC above 35 degC ambient, and an 85 degC standard limit. Egypt: about 40 degC normal, 50-55 degC above 35 degC ambient, and a 65 degC limit. Only Haier gives 'about 40 degC at 25 degC ambient', and GE/Haier pages count as one publisher. Drop 40, 50, 60-65 and 85 degC. The 'above 50 degC in a hot room' figure is supported by Haier (both pages) and, independently, by Igloo's 55 degC. The location of a rear coil rests on Haier Egypt plus a lifestyle site (Hunker); acceptable for a layout description. No source gives market shares for the layouts, so do not say which is most common.

safe_wording: In many refrigerators the compressor runs hot, well above room temperature, but some inverter-driven compressors can feel close to room temperature while they run.

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: Casing 'generally at a temperature between 85 ℃~90℃' listed as normal
'The compressor is hot. (When the compressor is working, it can reach a temperature of 194 °F, or 90 °C.)'
Compressor 'typically runs warm', 120-140 degF normal
'It's normal for your refrigerator compressor to be warm'
Inverter model: 'The compressor exterior may be room temperature while operating.'

problems: The numbers conflict. Haier and Igloo call 85-90 degC normal, while Sears says normal is 120-140 degF (49-60 degC) and that above 150 degF (66 degC) means overheating. Use no compressor temperature. The inverter exception rests on GE only, so phrase it as 'some'. It is not universal.

safe_wording: Heat flows on its own only from hotter to colder. Moving heat from a cold place to a warmer one takes work. Physicists call this the Clausius statement of the second law of thermodynamics.

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: Exact wording confirmed: 'It is not possible for heat to flow from a colder body to a warmer body without any work having been done to accomplish this flow.'
Clausius statement: impossible to build a cyclic device whose only effect is transferring heat from lower to higher temperature
'Macroscopically, heat appears to transfer thermal energy spontaneously in only one direction.'

problems: None. Say 'on its own', never 'can never'.

safe_wording: There is no 'cold' to add. Heat is energy that flows because of a temperature difference, and a refrigerator cools food by removing heat from it.

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: 'Heat is the spontaneous transfer of energy due to a temperature difference.'
'A household refrigerator removes heat from the food within it while exhausting heat to the surrounding air.'
Refrigerant evaporates and 'extract[s] energy from the cold area'

problems: 'No cold to add' is a framing line that follows from the definitions; no source states it literally.

safe_wording: A refrigerator works like a heat pump. It uses work, electrical energy driving a compressor, to move heat from a colder space to a warmer one.

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: 'Heat pumps, air conditioners, and refrigerators utilize heat transfer from cold to hot.'; 'The electrically driven compressor (work input W)...'
Internal energy will not spontaneously flow cold to hot; 'it can be forced to do so by doing work on the system.'

problems: OpenStax University Physics 4.3 treats refrigerators and heat pumps as related devices that differ in purpose; it does not say a refrigerator IS a heat pump. 'Works like' or 'is a kind of heat pump' is safe.

safe_wording: Inside the evaporator the refrigerant is kept at low pressure, so it boils, and boiling soaks up heat from inside the fridge.

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: 'Low pressure in the evaporator, caused by the suction of the compressor ... causes the liquid refrigerant to vaporize.' 'As the refrigerant vaporizes, it absorbs heat.'
'The coolant extracts heat from the refrigerator at the evaporator, causing coolant to vaporize.'
Refrigerant made to evaporate by lowering the pressure
Latent heat is 'approximately 95%' of the total heat absorbed (generic, not household-specific)

problems: The 95% latent share is from one generic heat-exchanger handbook (SWEP), not about household fridges. Drop the number. 'Mostly by boiling' is defensible but single-sourced; the safe wording avoids it.

safe_wording: The compressor squeezes the low-pressure vapor into a high-pressure vapor that is much hotter, hot enough to be well above room temperature. Compressor makers test household-type compressors at a condensing temperature of 54.4 °C (130 °F).

allowed_numbers.how_to_say_it: say it is a standard test condition for compressors ('rated at a condensing temperature of 130 °F'), not what every fridge runs at

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: 'The electrically driven compressor (work input W) raises the temperature and pressure of the gas'
'Compressor forces high temperature vapor into fan cooled tube and wire condenser.'
ASHRAE LBP: evaporating -23.3 degC (-10 degF), condensing 54.4 degC (130 degF)
ASHRAE LBP test: -23.3 degC evaporating, 54.4 degC condensing
ASHRAE LBP test column, condensing 54.4 degC

problems: The Samsung page is for compact applications, not stated as household fridges. The 32.2 degC ambient is Samsung-only, and Embraco's extracted ambient read 35 degC (garbled), so do not use an ambient figure.

safe_wording: In the condenser, the hot high-pressure vapor gives off its heat to the kitchen air and condenses back into a high-pressure liquid.

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: 'As heat is removed from the high-pressure vapor, it begins to condense into a high-pressure liquid.'
'heat transfer to the room occurs and the gas condenses to a liquid'
'Then it is compressed and forced to condense in the hot area'

safe_wording: Household refrigerators typically use a capillary tube, a long, very thin tube that restricts the flow and separates the high-pressure side from the low-pressure side. Past it, the pressure drops and the refrigerant starts to boil.

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: 'The capillary tube restricts the amount of refrigerant that leaves the condenser.'; part of the refrigerant vaporizes on exiting the capillary
Basic components include 'heat exchanger (capillary tube and suction line)'
Capillary in the refrigeration circuit

Refrigerant made to evaporate by lowering the pressure

problems: The 30% flash fraction is GE-only (see 3.10); drop it. 'Flash gas chills the rest of the liquid' has no second source (SWEP's compression-cycle page does not say it), so the safe wording leaves it out. SWEP and OpenStax describe a generic valve, not a capillary.

safe_wording: In many household refrigerators the capillary tube is soldered to the suction line returning to the compressor, forming a heat exchanger: the warm liquid in the capillary gives some of its heat to the cold vapor heading back to the compressor.

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: 'The heat exchange occurs where the capillary is soldered to the outside of the suction tube.' Also 'helps to prevent the suction tube from sweating.'
'To raise temperature of gas, suction line is placed in heat exchange with capillary.'
'heat exchanger (capillary tube and suction line)'

problems: The anti-sweating benefit is GE-only. Leave it out, or attribute it to GE's service guide. Say 'many', not 'household refrigerators' in general.

safe_wording: At normal atmospheric pressure the two common household refrigerants boil far below freezing: isobutane (R-600a) at about -12 °C (about 11 °F) and R-134a at about -26 °C (about -15 °F).

allowed_numbers.how_to_say_it: isobutane boils at about 11 °F (minus 12 °C)
R-134a boils at about minus 15 °F (minus 26 °C)

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: Isobutane Tboil 262 +/- 2 K (about -11 degC), average of 24 of 25 values
Boiling range 10.9 degF
-26.3 degC (-15.34 degF) at atmospheric pressure
-26.2 degC (-15.1 degF)

problems: Conversions check out (-11.78 degC = 10.8 degF; -26.3 degC = -15.3 degF). Round as shown. Note: the Wikiwand page contained an embedded prompt-injection instruction; it was ignored and does not affect the data.

safe_wording: The EPA approved isobutane for U.S. household refrigerators in 2011, with a charge limit of 57 grams per sealed system, and raised the limit for hydrocarbon refrigerants to 150 grams in 2018. Since January 1, 2025, new household refrigerators and freezers made or imported in the U.S. must use a refrigerant with a global warming potential of 150 or less, which rules out R-134a (about 1,430).

allowed_numbers.how_to_say_it: 57 grams, about 2 ounces, in 2011
150 grams from 2018
global warming potential of 150 or less
since the start of 2025
R-134a's is about 1,430

Household refrigerators and freezers: GWP limit 150, compliance January 1, 2025
Household hydrocarbon charge raised 'from 57 grams to 150 grams'
57 g to 150 g, in force Sept 7, 2018
Table row: Household refrigerators and freezers, 150, January 1, 2025

problems: The 2018 EPA fact sheet does not state 57 g or 150 g; the charge numbers rest on the Federal Register (57 g) plus ACHR News and IIR (both). EPA finalized Technology Transitions changes on May 26, 2026 (91 FR 31284). Secondary coverage shows no change for household refrigerators, but the final rule text was not read; recheck the EPA sector table before publishing.

safe_wording: Compressor makers rate household-type compressors under a standard test with the refrigerant boiling at about -23 °C (-10 °F) and condensing at about 54 °C (130 °F). Those are test conditions, not what every fridge runs at.

allowed_numbers.how_to_say_it: about minus 10 °F evaporating, as a test condition
about 130 °F condensing, as a test condition

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: ASHRAE LBP -23.3 degC / 54.4 degC
ASHRAE LBP test -23.3 / 54.4 degC; application range -35 to -10 degC for this one model
ASHRAE LBP test at -23.3 degC evaporating, 54.4 degC condensing

problems: The -35 to -10 degC range is one Embraco model; drop it or attribute it. 'Condenser surfaces typically about 40 degC in a 25 degC room' is Haier-only (two Haier pages = one publisher) and Haier's own pages disagree on other values; drop it. The 37-45 degC Bansal & Chin figures are refrigerant inlet temperatures from one test of one prototype, not surface temperatures; the COBEM paper is also inconsistent (says five tests, tabulates four; cites 2001 and 2002). Drop them.

safe_wording: Energy is conserved: the heat a fridge dumps into the kitchen equals the heat it pulls out of the food plus the electrical energy it uses. Engineers rate a refrigerator by its coefficient of performance, the heat removed divided by the work put in. On a standard compressor test, household compressor datasheets list figures of roughly 1.4 to 2.

allowed_numbers.how_to_say_it: heat out = heat removed + electrical energy in
heat removed divided by work in
under a harsh standard test, a household compressor moves roughly 1.4 to 2 units of heat for each unit of electricity

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: Qh = Qc + W; COP_ref = Qc/W; real refrigerators/ACs 'ranging from 2 to 6'
Heat delivered = heat extracted + work; for a refrigerator the useful quantity is heat extracted QC
EM R60CLP: 174 W capacity, 124 W input, COP 1.40 W/W at ASHRAE LBP (recomputed 174/124 = 1.40)
HTK80AA R-600a: COP 2.01-2.07 W/W at ASHRAE LBP; 1.64 W/W at EN 12900 Household

problems: The claim's 1.4 to 1.7 range is too narrow. A current Secop household-class compressor is rated at about 2.0 W/W at ASHRAE LBP, so the range is about 1.4 to 2. The KitchenAid figure (905 Btu/h / 3.412 / 153 W = 1.73) recomputes correctly, but the job aid gives no rating conditions, so it cannot be called 'under standard test conditions'; do not use it. OpenStax's 2-6 is a generic textbook range for whole devices; do not mix it with compressor ratings. These are compressor ratings, not whole-fridge real-use COP.

safe_wording: A liquid's boiling point depends on pressure. Lower the pressure and it boils at a lower temperature, which is why the low-pressure evaporator lets the refrigerant boil well below freezing, and the high-pressure condenser lets it condense above room temperature.

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: Boiling point above 100 degC at higher pressure (pressure cooker), below 100 degC at lower pressure (altitude)
'the boiling point of a liquid changes with the external pressure'; 'As the altitude increases, the boiling point decreases.'
'To change the evaporation temperature, the pressure must be changed.'
Refrigerant made to evaporate and condense by 'successively lowering and raising the pressure'

problems: OpenStax College Physics 13.5 (Phase Changes) could not be opened (permission request timed out); LibreTexts used instead.

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: 'Approximately 30% of the refrigerant will vaporize immediately upon exiting the capillary.'

problems: Quote confirmed, but only one source. My search for a second (household capillary flash-gas fraction) found none. The figure is physically plausible but depends on model and conditions.
fix_needed: Find an independent source (textbook worked example, ASHRAE/university paper or another manufacturer's service literature) that gives the flash-gas fraction at the capillary outlet of a household refrigerator, or drop the number. 3.4 already covers the mechanism without it.

safe_wording: For heat to flow out of the condenser on its own, the refrigerant inside must be hotter than the kitchen air. That is why the compressor has to push it well above room temperature.

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: 'The surrounding medium must be at a lower temperature than the condensing temperature of the refrigerant.'
Heat does not flow cold to hot without work
Clausius statement

problems: The '40 vs 25 degC' Haier example is single-publisher and inconsistent across Haier pages; do not use it.

safe_wording: Dust, lint and pet hair on the condenser block airflow and make it run hotter, so the compressor has to work harder and longer. Some manufacturers advise cleaning the coils: Hotpoint says at least once a year, and Whirlpool says every 3 to 6 months in homes with pets or a lot of dust. Some models don't need routine cleaning.

allowed_numbers.how_to_say_it: Hotpoint's guide says at least once a year
Whirlpool says every 3 to 6 months in homes with pets, heavy kitchen traffic or construction dust

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: 'Airflow blocked by lint, pet hair and dirt will cause the condenser and heat loop temperature to increase.'
Dirt on coils raises discharge pressure; compressor power rises; system must run longer (general air-cooled condensers)
'For most efficient operation, you need to keep the condenser clean.' 'at least once a year'

3 to 6 months for pets/traffic/construction dust; 'Some models do not require the condenser coils to be cleaned'; 'In a normal home operating environment, routine condenser cleaning is not typically needed.'
'Keep coils clean; make sure the door seals are airtight.'

problems: 'Newer' is unsupported; Whirlpool says only 'some models'. problems: The Samsung figure is from Samsung Canada; U.S. manuals may differ. Do not present 1/8 in and 5 cm as the absolute extremes of the market.

safe_wording: Putting a refrigerator next to an oven, a dishwasher, a heating vent or in direct sunlight makes it harder for it to shed heat, and energy-saving guides and installation instructions say to avoid it.

allowed_numbers.how_to_say_it: optional, attributed: one Frigidaire service manual says not to install where the room drops below 60 °F or rises above 110 °F

Out of direct sunlight, away from range/dishwasher; not below 60 degF or above 110 degF

problems: The 60-110 degF range is one manufacturer's install limit; use only with attribution. No source quantifies the energy penalty.

safe_wording: Frost builds up on the evaporator because its surface stays below freezing, and moisture in the air inside, from food and from warm, humid air that comes in when the door opens, condenses and freezes on it.

confirmed_sources.what_it_confirms: Household evaporator surface 'always below the freezing point of the water'; 'The air dragged from the cabinets, contains moisture'

'Uncovered foods release moisture and make the compressor work harder.'
Adaptive defrost interval shortens with door-open time (indirect evidence)

problems: 'Especially' door openings is stronger than the household evidence. INTARCON is about commercial cold rooms; GE's logic is indirect. Present door openings as one source of moisture, not the main one.

safe_wording: Frost conducts heat very poorly, so a layer of it insulates the evaporator and chokes the airflow, cutting how well the fridge cools and wasting energy.

problems: All the numbers are confirmed and the arithmetic holds (103.1 / 1,305 = 7.9%). But every source is EIA, which counts as one publisher, and my search found no independent second source for refrigerators' share of U.S. household electricity. The 2020 percentage is the researcher's own calculation, not an EIA-stated figure; EIA's stated figure is 7% from RECS 2015.
fix_needed: Either find an independent source (DOE/LBNL, ACEEE, ASAP or a peer-reviewed end-use study) stating refrigerators' share of U.S. household electricity, or have the orchestrator decide whether official federal survey statistics may stand on the primary source alone. If that exception is granted, the safe wording would be: 'According to the EIA, refrigerators use about 7 percent of the electricity in American homes.' The same decision would unlock 6.1's 617 kWh average.
